sections.h2: What should I know about selling a house in University City, MO?
sections.html:
University City is an inner-ring suburb of St. Louis in St. Louis County, and its housing stock is older than most of the county around it. The city has a rule that matters to every seller: a house sold or rented here needs a city occupancy permit before anyone moves in, and the city suggests arranging the inspection before you list. Plan around that step early, because it shapes repairs, timing and what a buyer, whether a family or an investor, has to do after closing.

The Census Bureau counted 35,065 residents in 2020 and estimates 34,657 for July 1, 2025, a drop of 1.6 percent from the 2020 estimates base. Streetcar-era blocks in the south and postwar blocks in the north sit within a few miles of each other, so condition and layout vary from one street to the next.

sections.h2: What kind of city is University City, and how does that affect a sale?
sections.html:
University City is a streetcar suburb. According to Wikipedia, the older southern portion keeps much of its historic architecture, especially around Delmar Boulevard, while the northern part developed mostly after World War II and has more shopping centers and car-oriented development. A buyer looking at a 1920s house south of Delmar is comparing different things than a buyer looking at a postwar house north of Olive.

The city was incorporated in September 1906 after publisher Edward Gardner Lewis bought 85 acres northwest of Forest Park and built a model town. His octagonal Magazine Building, a 135-foot tower, is now City Hall at 6801 Delmar Boulevard. Between 1910 and 1920 the city grew faster than any other in Missouri, and the biggest wave of housing construction came after World War II.

The city covers 5.9 square miles and is bounded roughly by Skinker Boulevard on the east and Interstate 170 on the west. Heman Park, at 85 acres, and the Ruth Park golf course are the largest green spaces. Midland Boulevard runs along the divide between the Mississippi and Missouri River watersheds, and the River Des Peres rises near the University City and Clayton line.

sections.h2: Do I need an occupancy inspection to sell my house in University City?
sections.html:
Yes, plan on one. The city says anyone moving into University City must apply for and receive an occupancy permit before moving in, and that anyone planning to sell should arrange an inspection before the house goes on the market. The inspection fee for a home sale is $80 per unit.

  • Applications go to the Department of Planning and Zoning on the fourth floor of City Hall, 6801 Delmar Boulevard, or by email to inspections@ucitymo.org.
  • The application fee is $25 and is not refundable. Card payments carry a 3.25 percent convenience fee.
  • Inspectors check electrical, plumbing, heating and general building condition against the property maintenance code.
  • A valid driver's license, state ID or passport is accepted as identification.

If the house fails, the city requires corrections. For minor repairs it may issue a conditional occupancy permit for $35, which gives the owner 60 days to finish the work while people live there. If the work is not done in 60 days, the city can declare the occupancy invalid and take legal action against the owner and occupants.

sections.h2: What are my options for selling a house in University City?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or take an offer from an investor who buys houses as they stand. Each route runs into the same occupancy requirement, so ask each buyer who will order the inspection and who pays for repairs.

  • List on the market. You pay the inspection fee, fix what the inspector flags, and ask your agent for the commission rate and the likely closing timeline.
  • Sell it yourself. You save an agent's fee but handle pricing, showings, the contract and the city paperwork.
  • Sell to an investor. A buyer paying cash is not waiting on a lender. Compare the offer against what the house would net after repairs, the inspection and closing costs on a listing.

A house with a failed inspection, a tenant who will not leave, or an inherited estate still in probate can be harder to list. Those are the situations where investor offers tend to come up. Get at least two written offers and read what each says about who pays closing costs.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work when I sell in University City?
sections.html:
University City sits in St. Louis County, so the county Collector of Revenue bills the tax and the County Assessor values the house. Taxes must be paid or postmarked by December 31 of the year they are billed. After that, the Collector's FAQ says interest of up to 18 percent a year and a 2 percent penalty apply under RSMo chapters 139 and 140.

The Assessor reassesses all real estate every odd-numbered year, so 2027 is the next reassessment. For appeals, the Board of Equalization takes filings from May 1 to the second Monday in July; the 2026 deadline of July 13 has passed, and the next window opens May 1, 2027. The Collector's office is at 41 S. Central Avenue in Clayton and answers at (314) 615-7100. If your account is behind, the back tax team at (314) 615-7865 can give the payoff and explain redemption limits.

Programs worth asking about include the county's Senior Property Tax Freeze and the state Property Tax Credit, often called the Circuit Breaker. Ask the title company for a payoff figure before you set a closing date so unpaid tax is settled from your proceeds.

sections.h2: What else should a University City seller check?
sections.html:
Schools are run by the School District of University City, which has University City High School, and many families shop by district. The district is separate from other school systems in the St. Louis area, so mention it in your listing.

Ask your title company which county office records the deed and what it needs from you. Cancel utilities after closing and leave the keys and any permit paperwork for the buyer. If you rent the house out now, confirm the occupancy permit status before the buyer closes.

  • Gather the last occupancy permit, any repair receipts and warranties.
  • Check for open permits on past additions or finished basements.
  • Ask your title company about unpaid city or county charges before listing.

faqs.q: Does University City require an inspection to sell a house?
faqs.a: The city asks sellers to arrange an inspection before listing, and the buyer or tenant must hold an occupancy permit before moving in. The fee for a sale inspection is $80 per unit, plus a $25 application fee.

faqs.q: What happens if my University City house fails the occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: The city requires corrections. For minor issues it can issue a conditional permit for $35 that gives you 60 days to finish repairs. If the work is not done in that time, the permit can be voided.

faqs.q: When are St. Louis County property taxes due for a University City house?
faqs.a: They are due by December 31 of the billing year, and payments postmarked later carry interest and a penalty. The 2026 bill follows the same date, so settle any balance through your title company at closing.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal my University City assessment this year?
faqs.a: No. The 2026 Board of Equalization deadline was July 13, and it has passed. Filings for the next cycle open May 1, 2027, and the county reassesses in odd-numbered years.

faqs.q: Is University City mostly owners or renters?
faqs.a: About 56.2 percent of homes are owner-occupied according to the Census Bureau, so a large share of buyers are landlords. Median value of owner-occupied homes is $306,700 for 2020 to 2024.
